body.p: Claims 1-11 and 14-19 are amended for clarity. New claim 20 is added. Support for claim 20 may be found in original claim 1. The specification is amended to correct several clerical errors and to be consistent with claim expressions. Applicant respectfully requests favorable reconsideration.
Examiner Interview
Applicant expresses appreciation to Examiner Lopez for discussing the pending

application and Office Action with Applicant's attorney on January 24, 2025. The deficiencies in the cited prior art, particularly the Langevin and Ellingson references, were presented. Regrettably, Examiner Lopez confessed he had insufficient time to consider Applicant's interpretation of the prior art and the deficiencies of his "result effective variable" legal theories advanced in the Office Action. No agreement was reached.
Claim Objections

The Office objected to claims 1, 6-8, 10, 18, and 19 because of minor informalities. The claims have been amended to address the informalities. Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the claim objections.
The Office rejected claims 1-4, 6-8, and 17-19 under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) as being

indefinite. The claims have been amended to provide proper antecedent basis and clarity to address the issues identified in the Office Action. Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b).

The Office rejected claims 1, 5, and 9 under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Clarke (U.S. Patent No. 4,447,235) in view of Ellingson (U.S. Patent No. 6,217,556) and Langevin (U.S. Patent No. 6,156,019).

The Office based these rejections on the application of legal precedent that the claimed inner cross sectional area is a "result effective variable" that would have been obvious to "optimize." Applicant respectfully submits that the present facts do not support proper application of the asserted legal precedent. MPEP 2144 states that legal precedent may be used to support obviousness only if the facts of the case are sufficiently similar to those of the application.

The Office acknowledges that Clarke fails to disclose that the recited inlet, blood sample, and waste fluid passages have an inner cross-sectional area in the range from 0.3 to 2.0 square millimeters. The Office cited Langevin (Col. 5, lines 58-63) as disclosing the second channel 10 having an inner cross-sectional area from 0.3 to 2.0 square millimeters.

As shown in Langevin's Fig. lA, Langevin's second channel 10 does not correspond to the claimed "inlet fluid passage," "blood sample fluid passage," and "waste fluid passage" of the stopcock body. Langevin discloses second channel 10 bypassing at least two 3-way stopcocks, the three-way stopcock 5 and the double barreled stopcock 7. Thus, Langevin clearly discloses that the second channel 10 is not intended to correspond to any fluid passage of a 3-way stopcock.

Recognizing this deficiency, the Office argues that the cross-sectional area of the "inlet fluid passage," "blood sample fluid passage," and "waste fluid passage" is a "result effective variable" that can be optimized and modified as a matter of "routine optimization." Applicant respectfully disagrees for at least two reasons.
First, the Office has failed to establish that the cross-sectional area of the "inlet fluid

passage," "blood sample fluid passage," and "waste fluid passage" is a result effective variable. The Office has merely established that the cross-sectional area of Langevin's second channel 10 can be modified to control the flow rate through Langevin's second channel 10. However, Langevin's second channel 10 is not an "inlet fluid passage," "blood sample fluid passage," and "waste fluid passage" of a microvolume 3-way stopcock. Therefore, there is no evidence in the record that Langevin recognized the cross-sectional area of the "inlet fluid passage," "blood sample fluid passage," and "waste fluid passage" to be a result effective variable.

Second, a person skilled in the art of fluid dynamics understands when one fluid channel is divided into two parallel fluid channels, as disclosed by Langevin, that the flow rate within the divided channels is controlled by the cross-sectional area of the respective fluid channels. This principle is relevant to Langevin's device, but it is irrelevant to the presently claimed invention which does not utilize parallel fluid flow channels. Thus, cross-sectional area may be a result effective variable in the parallel fluid flow structure of Langevin, but it is NOT a result effective variable in the "inlet fluid passage," "blood sample fluid passage," and "waste fluid passage" of Applicant's claimed microvolume 3-way stopcock.
The Office has failed to clearly articulate why a person having ordinary skill in the art would have modified the cross-sectional area of Clarke's "inlet fluid passage," "blood sample
fluid passage," and "waste fluid passage" based upon the Langevin's second channel 10. Therefore, the Office has failed to establish prima facie obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103.

Regarding claim 5, claim 1 has been amended to expressly recite the cannula insert, the blood sample cone, and the waste cone. The Office Action asserted that Clarke's adapter 29 fixed to the proximate end 27 of the catheter 23 (Clarke, col. 3, lines 2-3) corresponds to the "cannula insert". Applicant respectfully disagrees. Clarke's catheter adapter 29 is merely the structure located at the proximate end 27 of the catheter 23 which enables the catheter to be snugly fit on the exterior surface of the arm 33. It is not disposed within the inlet fluid passage; instead, it is essentially a female connector disposed on the exterior of the male connector (arm 33).

The Office Action further asserts that Clark's connector 48 located at the proximate end of the needle 45 (Clarke, col. 3, lines 42-44) corresponds to the "blood sample cone." Applicant respectfully disagrees. Clarke's connector 48 is merely the adapter structure which enables the needle to be attached to the hollow projection 50 at the end of a syringe 47, 49. It is not disposed within the blood sample fluid passage; instead, it is essentially a female connector disposed on the exterior of the male connector (hollow projection 50 at the end of syringe 49).

The Office Action further asserts that Clarke's adapter 83 used to connect tube 82 to the side arm 59 (Clarke, col. 5, lines 12-16; Fig. 1) corresponds to the "waste cone." Applicant respectfully disagrees. Clarke's adapter 83 is merely the structure which enables the tube 82 to be snugly fit on the exterior surface of the arm 59. It is not disposed within the waste fluid passage; instead, it is essentially a female connector disposed on the exterior of the male connector (arm 59).

The Office has failed to identify any structures in the cited prior art which reasonably correspond to the claimed cannula insert, blood sample cone, and waste cone. Applicant respectfully submits that amended claim 1 would not have been obvious under 35 U.S.C. 103 from Clarke in view of Ellingson and Langevin. Applicant respectfully requests withdrawal of the rejection and allowance of claim 1 and its respective dependent claims 2-4, 6-10, and 20.

The Office rejected claims 10-12 and 14-19 under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Ellingson in view of Jho (U.S. Publication No. 2018/0207398) and Altman. These claims are directed to a specific method for obtaining a clean blood specimen. Ellingson in view of Jho and Altman fail to disclose the specifically claimed method. Ellingson in view of Jho and Altman disclose some apparatus elements that may be manipulated in different methods, but the claimed method for obtaining a clean blood specimen is not disclosed or suggested in the cited prior art.
